After walking the sacred journeys, lift your eyes to the whole world the gospel now covers. The world-faith map (Part VIII) carries the same dataset the live site woven into its Interlinked Bible module: seven tradition categories across 175 countries, on a total population of 8.23 billion.

Each entry follows the same structure: Context; the mainstream position with primary sources; a Christian apologetic response; and points for respectful discussion — because a debate opponent who feels straw-manned will not listen, no matter how strong the argument is.

Each profile in the atlas carries its own distinct artwork — sourced historical images where they exist, and text-guided reconstructions strictly limited to the forms the Bible or 1 Enoch describes. Concept and claim rows carry no images, so no picture pretends to be evidence.

Each question below comes with a plain answer, a verse from the King James Bible, and five responses from different Christian traditions. Where a tradition has a famous quotation to offer, it is included.

Every prophecy on the live prophecy map carries three ways of reading it. The historical view looks at what happened in the past. The metaphorical view sees a spiritual meaning in Christ. The futurist view waits for a literal fulfillment still to come. This way you can see which school of theology counts each prophecy as complete.

Every row is one person's life; where lives overlap, those people were alive together. Ages in Genesis 5 and 11 (Hebrew text; the Septuagint differs) give absolute dates for the antediluvian and early postdiluvian patriarchs. From Judah onward Scripture lists names but not ages, and Matthew's list skips some generations, so those bars are estimates built from known reign dates and generation spacing (shown as approx). Enoch is shown to age 365, when God took him. Chronology is Ussher-style years from creation (AM).

The Interlinked Bible / cross-reference module maps every verse of the King James Version against openbible.info's topical links — 66 books, with chapter and verse counts used to lay out the classic chord diagram.
The world map module ships dominant-tradition polygons for 175 countries with population and percentage shares — the same data tabulated earlier in Part 7.

These are the biblical Psalms put into classical Punjabi meters by Imam-ud-Din Shahbaz in 1908. Each one is listed with its raga and its English theme. The full hymn texts live at punjabizaboor1908.com.

These eight maps show real places on true geography. On the website you can press a button and watch footsteps trace each route, stop by stop. The coastlines come from Natural Earth, which is free for everyone to use. The routes follow standard scholarly reconstructions, so a few details are approximate. Use them to picture where these stories actually happened.

This is a living archive of Pakistani Christian music. It follows four generations of one family, beginning with a founding pastor in Montgomery, which is now called Sahiwal, and running through to today's composers and maestros.
